motions.outcome: passed with a unanimous vote of 4:0.
motions.headline: Consent agenda approved
motions.summary: The council approved its consent agenda, noting a $47,930 change order on one item and pulling another item for no action.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for residents — the consent agenda is the batch of routine items the council passes together in a single vote.

motions.item_title: Approve the appointment of Jessi Call as a Youth Council Committee Advisor beginning immediatel…
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to approve the appointment of Jessi Call as a Youth Council Committee Advisor beginning immediately through June 30, 2026. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.outcome: passed with a unanimous vote of 4:0.
motions.headline: Jessi Call named Youth Council advisor
motions.summary: The council appointed Jessi Call as an advisor to the Youth Council Committee, effective immediately and running through June 30, 2026.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for residents — this is an appointment to the committee that guides the city's youth council.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Cedar Corners Phase 5 Development Agreement
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Cedar Corners Phase 5 Development Agreement with the following additions: 1. That the applicant work with Planning staff on establishing a benchmark for when construction can be started; 2. That the pedestrian rights of way are connecting, and the two roads are connecting on either side of Poplar Drive and Maple Street. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Cedar Corners Phase 5 development deal approved
motions.summary: The city approved a development agreement for Cedar Corners Phase 5, with conditions on when construction may start and on connecting the roads and sidewalks.
motions.impact: If you live near Poplar Drive or Maple Street, the developer must connect the roads on both sides and keep the walkways continuous rather than leaving them to dead-end.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Cedar Corners Phase 5 from Residential to RC Zone
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Cedar Corners Phase 5 from Residential to RC Zone. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Cedar Corners Phase 5 rezoned to RC
motions.summary: The council changed the zoning on the Cedar Corners Phase 5 land from residential to the city's RC zone.
motions.impact: This is the zoning step behind the Cedar Corners Phase 5 project. If you live nearby, what can be built on that land is now governed by RC zone rules instead of the old residential rules.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Cedar Corners Phase 5 from Neighborhood Residential 1 to Neighborhood Residential 2
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Cedar Corners Phase 5 from Neighborhood Residential 1 to Neighborhood Residential 2. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Land use map updated for Cedar Corners Phase 5
motions.summary: The council changed the city's long-range land use map for Cedar Corners Phase 5 from Neighborhood Residential 1 to Neighborhood Residential 2.
motions.impact: This updates the city's long-term plan for that land so it matches the rezoning approved the same night. Nothing changes anywhere else in the city.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Cedar Valley Holbrook
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to table an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Cedar Valley Holbrook. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Cedar Valley Holbrook rezoning put on hold
motions.summary: The council delayed a decision on rezoning the land known as Cedar Valley Holbrook.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for now. The proposal is set aside and has to come back to the council before anything about that land is decided.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Cedar Valley Holbrook
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to table an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Cedar Valley Holbrook. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Cedar Valley Holbrook land use change delayed
motions.summary: The council delayed a decision on changing the long-range land use map for the land known as Cedar Valley Holbrook.
motions.impact: Nothing changes — this map change was set aside along with the related rezoning and will return to the council later.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Projects for the Fiscal Year 2026 as follows: • PUBLIC SERVICE PROJECTS: o LMI Cemetery Services Assistance - $5,000 o LMI Utility Assistance - $15,000 o Senior Assistance Program - $3,000 o LMI Back-to-School Drive - $5,000 o Tabitha’s Way Food Pantry - $7,292 ▪ TOTALS: $35,292 • OTHER PROJECTS: o LMI Yard Cleanup - $36,163.20 o ADA Ramp/Crosswalk Installation at Fiona St/Airport Rd - $20,000 o Small Business Grants - $150,000 • TOTALS: $206,163.20 Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Projects for the Fiscal Year 2026 as follows: • PUBLIC SERVICE PROJECTS: o LMI Cemetery Services Assistance - $5,000 o LMI Utility Assistance - $15,000 o Senior Assistance Program - $3,000 o LMI Back-to-School Drive - $5,000 o Tabitha’s Way Food Pantry - $7,292 ▪ TOTALS: $35,292 • OTHER PROJECTS: o LMI Yard Cleanup - $36,163.20 o ADA Ramp/Crosswalk Installation at Fiona St/Airport Rd - $20,000 o Small Business Grants - $150,000 • TOTALS: $206,163.20 Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Block grant money set: $150K for small businesses
motions.summary: The city set its 2026 federal block grant spending: $150,000 in small business grants, $36,163 for yard cleanup, $20,000 for an ADA crosswalk, and $35,292 in aid programs.
motions.impact: Small businesses can apply for grant money, and lower-income households get help with utility bills, cemetery costs, school supplies, food and yard cleanup. A new ADA ramp and crosswalk is funded at Fiona Street and Airport Road.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Fee Reduction Request of Brett Simpson for a Master Development Plan Amendment Application from $3,350 to $1,350
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to waive the fee for Brett Simpson’s Gazelle Run Master Development Plan Amendment Application. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion. Councilmembers sought clarification on the intended use of the fee and collectively expressed that the fee should be reduced rather than fully waived. AMENDED MOTION: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Fee Reduction Request of Brett Simpson for a Master Development Plan Amendment Application from $3,350 to $1,350. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Gazelle Run application fee cut to $1,350
motions.summary: The council cut the fee for Brett Simpson's Gazelle Run master development plan amendment from $3,350 to $1,350, rather than waiving it entirely as first proposed.
motions.impact: This touches one applicant only. The city collects $2,000 less on this single application, and the fees everyone else pays are unchanged.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Expressing an Intent to Work in Partnership with the West Traverse Sentinel Landscape (WTSL) Committee for the Relocation of the Eagle Mountain City Rodeo Grounds within the Army Compatible Use Buffer (ACUB) Area Surrounding Camp Williams
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Expressing an Intent to Work in Partnership with the West Traverse Sentinel Landscape (WTSL) Committee for the Relocation of the Eagle Mountain City Rodeo Grounds within the Army Compatible Use Buffer (ACUB) Area Surrounding Camp Williams. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.outcome: passed with a unanimous vote of 4:0.
motions.headline: City backs moving the rodeo grounds
motions.summary: The council declared its intent to work with the West Traverse Sentinel Landscape committee on relocating the city rodeo grounds into the buffer area around Camp Williams.
motions.impact: Nothing moves yet — this only commits the city to work with the partner group on a possible new site. If you use the rodeo grounds, expect a relocation plan to come back for a real decision later.

motions.item_title: Table the McDonald's (City Center) Site Plan to require completion of a traffic study prior to…
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to table the McDonald's (City Center) Site Plan to require completion of a traffic study prior to approval. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: McDonald's plan paused for a traffic study
motions.summary: The council put the McDonald's site plan at City Center on hold until a traffic study is completed.
motions.impact: The City Center McDonald's cannot be approved until traffic near the site is studied, so the project is pushed back. Nothing changes on the ground in the meantime.

motions.item_title: (see motion text for included items)
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve the Consent Agenda removing Items 10.A, 11.B., and 11.C., and placing them on the scheduled items for further discussion. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Consent agenda approved, three items pulled
motions.summary: The council approved its consent agenda after pulling three items out of the bundle for separate discussion later in the meeting.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for residents — this is the batch of routine items the council passes in a single vote, with the three pulled items taken up on their own.

motions.item_title: The Completed Section of the Legislative Priority List and also add Design of City Hall and oth…
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved that the City Hall Land Acquisition and Mortgage Assistance Program items be moved to the Completed Section of the Legislative Priority List and also add Design of City Hall and other uses within Phase 1 of the Downtown Plan as a High Priority to the list. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: City hall design made a top city priority
motions.summary: The council moved the city hall land purchase and a mortgage assistance program to its completed list and made designing a city hall a high priority downtown.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for you yet. This is the city's internal to-do list, and it now flags designing a city hall within the first phase of the downtown plan as a top item.

motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved authorize staff to begin analysis and preparation for a potential future action to place a Recreation, Arts, and Parks (RAP) Sales Tax question on the 2025 Municipal Election ballot. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Possible parks and arts sales tax on 2025 ballot
motions.summary: The council took up a proposal to have staff study placing a Recreation, Arts and Parks (RAP) sales tax question on the 2025 city election ballot.
motions.impact: Nothing changes now — this is only analysis. If the council later moves ahead, you would get the final say on the tax at the 2025 municipal election.

motions.item_title: Adopt implementation of the MBR technology solution and the use of CM/CG construction methodolo…
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to adopt implementation of the MBR technology solution and the use of CM/CG construction methodology for the proposed sewer treatment facility. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Sewer plant to use membrane treatment technology
motions.summary: The city settled on membrane bioreactor (MBR) treatment technology and a construction-manager delivery method for its proposed new sewer treatment plant.
motions.impact: This locks in how the planned sewer plant will clean wastewater and how it gets built. Nothing changes on your bill today — the motion names no cost or timeline.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Supporting the Creation of a Utah Inland Port Authority Project Area in Eagle Mountain City
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Supporting the Creation of a Utah Inland Port Authority Project Area in Eagle Mountain City. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.outcome: failed for lack of majority vote; 2:3.
motions.headline: Inland port project area rejected
motions.summary: The council turned down a resolution supporting the creation of a state Inland Port Authority project area inside Eagle Mountain.
motions.impact: No inland port district moves forward with the city's backing, so the industrial development and tax arrangements that come with one are off the table for now. Day to day, nothing changes.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Title 17, Zoning as presented in the updated packet
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to adopt An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Title 17, Zoning as presented in the updated packet. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Changes to the city zoning code adopted
motions.summary: The council amended Title 17, the city's zoning code, adopting the updated version included in the meeting packet.
motions.impact: Zoning rules govern what can be built on a property and where. The motion itself doesn't spell out what changed, so the effect on any given property isn't clear from the record.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Big Eagle 7 to industrial base zoning and apply the RTI overlay zone
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to adopt An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as Big Eagle 7 to industrial base zoning and apply the RTI overlay zone. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Big Eagle 7 land rezoned for industrial use
motions.summary: The council rezoned the land known as Big Eagle 7 to industrial zoning and applied an RTI overlay zone on top of it.
motions.impact: This land is now set aside for industrial use rather than homes. If you live near Big Eagle 7, what gets built there in the future will be industrial.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Big Eagle 7
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the General Plan Future Land Use Map for Certain Lands Known as Big Eagle 7. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Long-range land use map updated for Big Eagle 7
motions.summary: The council amended the General Plan's future land use map for the land known as Big Eagle 7.
motions.impact: The General Plan is the city's long-term blueprint for what goes where. This redraws that map for the Big Eagle 7 area; nothing on the ground changes immediately.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Releasing a Permanent Sanitary Sewer Easement and Retaining a Temporary Sanitary Sewer Easement
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Releasing a Permanent Sanitary Sewer Easement and Retaining a Temporary Sanitary Sewer Easement. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Permanent sewer easement released, temporary one kept
motions.summary: The council gave up a permanent sewer easement across a property while holding on to a temporary one.
motions.impact: This is a property-records step between the city and one landowner. The motion doesn't say where the easement is, and nothing changes for residents generally.

motions.item_title: Approve the UTA Park and ride Site Plan as presented
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to approve the UTA Park and ride Site Plan as presented. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: UTA park-and-ride site plan approved
motions.summary: The council approved the site plan for a UTA park-and-ride lot in Eagle Mountain.
motions.impact: The transit agency can move ahead with a lot where you would park and catch a bus. The motion gives no location, size, or opening date.

Councilmember Gray requested that the correction to the minutes be included in the motion. AMENDED MOTION: Councilmember Wright moved to approve the Consent Agenda removing 14.A. to be addressed in the scheduled items and including the adjustments to the March 18, 2025 minutes as noted from Councilmember Gray in the Work Session. motions.headline: Consent agenda approved, one item pulled
motions.summary: The council approved its consent agenda, pulling item 14.A. out for separate discussion and folding in a correction to the March 18 minutes.
motions.impact: Routine housekeeping — nothing changes for residents. This is the single batch vote the council uses to clear uncontested items at once.

motions.item_title: Approve the appointment of Marian Burningham for a three year term, through December 31, 2027,…
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to approve the appointment of Marian Burningham for a three year term, through December 31, 2027, to the Cemetery Advisory Board. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Marian Burningham appointed to Cemetery Advisory Board
motions.summary: The council appointed Marian Burningham to a three-year term on the Cemetery Advisory Board, running through December 31, 2027.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for residents — the board advises the city on the cemetery, and this simply fills a seat on it.

motions.item_title: Adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming April as Financial Literacy Month
motions.motion: Councilmember Gray moved to adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming April as Financial Literacy Month. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: April named Financial Literacy Month
motions.summary: The council proclaimed April as Financial Literacy Month in Eagle Mountain.
motions.impact: Ceremonial only — nothing changes for residents, and no city money or program is committed.

motions.item_title: Adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming April 25, 2025 as Arbor Day
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming April 25, 2025 as Arbor Day. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Arbor Day set for April 25
motions.summary: The council proclaimed April 25, 2025 as Arbor Day in Eagle Mountain.
motions.impact: Ceremonial only — nothing changes for residents. It's a symbolic nod to tree planting, with no new rules or spending attached.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving an Agreement with the Valley Crossroads Chamber of Commerce for the ShopFestTM Utah event
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving an Agreement with the Valley Crossroads Chamber of Commerce for the ShopFestTM Utah Event with the following changes: 1. In section five, changing the word “Chamber” to the word “City”, 2. In section ten, changing the term from five years to ten years, ending in 2035, 3. Add a “meet to confer” provision, 4. Change signature from Melissa Clark to Matt Everett, Chamber Treasurer, and 5. All future provisions for amendments to be in writing. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: ShopFest Utah agreement extended to 2035
motions.summary: The council took up an agreement with the Valley Crossroads Chamber of Commerce to run the ShopFest Utah event, lengthening the term from five years to ten, through 2035.
motions.impact: Nothing changes day to day. This sets the terms under which the chamber puts on ShopFest, and commits the city to that arrangement through 2035 rather than 2030.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the First Amendment to the Eagle Quest East Master Development Agreement This item was discussed before Item 12.A.
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to adopt a Resolution Approving the First Amendment to the Eagle Quest East Master Development Agreement. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Change to the Eagle Quest East development deal
motions.summary: The council approved the first amendment to the master development agreement covering the Eagle Quest East project.
motions.impact: The motion does not spell out what changed. A master development agreement sets the ground rules for how a project area gets built, so this matters mainly to the developer and to people living near Eagle Quest East.

motions.item_title: Deny the Harmony 14 Preliminary Plat
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to deny the Harmony 14 Preliminary Plat. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Vote to deny the Harmony 14 subdivision plan
motions.summary: The council considered rejecting the preliminary plat — the proposed lot layout — for the Harmony 14 subdivision.
motions.impact: This is the step where the city signs off on how a subdivision is laid out, so it affects the Harmony 14 developer and anyone living near the site. The record here gives no reasons.

motions.item_title: Deny the Preliminary Plat, Harmony 13
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to deny the Preliminary Plat, Harmony 13. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Harmony 13 subdivision plan denied
motions.summary: The council rejected the preliminary plat — the proposed lot layout — for the Harmony 13 subdivision.
motions.impact: As drawn, Harmony 13 does not move forward. That touches the developer and neighbors near the site; the motion itself gives no reasons for the denial.

motions.item_title: Table the Master Site Plan for Pinnacles B-3
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to table the Master Site Plan for Pinnacles B-3. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Pinnacles B-3 site plan put on hold
motions.summary: The council set the master site plan for Pinnacles B-3 aside without deciding it.
motions.impact: Nothing is settled either way — the plan can come back to the council later. If you live near the Pinnacles area, this only delays the decision.

motions.item_title: (see motion text for included items)
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve the Consent Agenda removing items 12.A., 12.B., 12.C. and 13.C. from the agenda and moving them to the scheduled items. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Consent agenda approved, four items pulled
motions.summary: The council approved its consent agenda after pulling items 12.A, 12.B, 12.C and 13.C out for separate discussion.
motions.impact: Routine housekeeping — nothing changes for residents. The four pulled items were debated one at a time instead of being passed in a batch.

motions.item_title: Adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming March 2025 as Multiple Sclerosis…
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Proclamation of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Proclaiming March 2025 as Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Awareness Month. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.headline: March named MS Awareness Month
motions.summary: The council proclaimed March 2025 as Multiple Sclerosis Awareness Month in Eagle Mountain.
motions.impact: This is a ceremonial statement — nothing changes for residents, and no city money or rules are involved.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Supporting the Creation of a Utah Inland Port Authority Project Area in Eagle Mountain City

motions.impact: This mostly matters to landowners and developers: it opens a path to shift allowed homes off one parcel and onto another, which means density can land in different places than the base zoning suggests.

motions.summary: The council amended the city's storm water ordinance, the rules covering runoff and drainage.
motions.impact: The motion doesn't say what changed, so it points to no specific effect on residents. Rules like these mainly govern builders and how new development handles runoff.

motions.summary: The city changed the rules for the water rights new residential developments must provide before they can build.
motions.impact: This lands on developers bringing new homes to the city, and on how much water the city banks as it grows. The motion doesn't spell out whether the requirement went up or down.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 17.25 Residential Zones with the following changes: 1. EMMC 17.25.020(E)(2)(a)(iv) and 17.25.020(F)(1)(a)(iv) are changed to, “Deed Restrictions: A deed restriction shall be recorded for the property dedicated as a moderate income dwelling unit that establishes the unit shall be occupied by the owner and priced for a household with a gross income equal to or less than 80% of the median gross income for Utah County;” and 2. EMMC 17.25.020(E)(2)(a)(i) and 17.25.020(F)(1)(a)(i) are changed to, “Required Amount of Moderate Income Housing: A minimum of 10% of new residential development in this zone shall be dedicated to moderate income housing (MIH) units priced for occupancy by households with a gross income equal to or less than 80% of the median gross income for Utah County per Utah Code 10-9a-103.” Councilmember Gray seconded the motion
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 17.25 Residential Zones with the following changes: 1. EMMC 17.25.020(E)(2)(a)(iv) and 17.25.020(F)(1)(a)(iv) are changed to, “Deed Restrictions: A deed restriction shall be recorded for the property dedicated as a moderate income dwelling unit that establishes the unit shall be occupied by the owner and priced for a household with a gross income equal to or less than 80% of the median gross income for Utah County;” and 2. EMMC 17.25.020(E)(2)(a)(i) and 17.25.020(F)(1)(a)(i) are changed to, “Required Amount of Moderate Income Housing: A minimum of 10% of new residential development in this zone shall be dedicated to moderate income housing (MIH) units priced for occupancy by households with a gross income equal to or less than 80% of the median gross income for Utah County per Utah Code 10-9a-103.” Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: 10% of new homes in some zones must be affordable
motions.summary: The city now requires at least 10% of new homes in certain residential zones to be priced for households earning 80% or less of Utah County's median income.
motions.impact: If you build or buy in these zones, a share of the homes carry a recorded deed restriction: the owner must live there and the price is capped. Applies to new development, not existing homes.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Establishing a Mortgage Assistance Program.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to approve a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting a Mortgage Assistance Program with the following changes: 1. Amend the maximum loan amount to $25,000; 2. Amend to indicate there is no maximum to the applicant(s)’ cash contribution to the purchase of a property; 3. Amend to indicate there is no minimum or maximum to the applicant(s)’ liquid assets at closing; 4. Amend the maximum Area Median Income to $151,800 for households of 6 or more; 5. Amend the application prioritization and schedule as presented: Namely to reflect prioritization by applicant employment type then prioritization by income relative to area median income with lower income households receiving higher priority; 6. Extend the requirement to respond to applicants regarding minimum qualifications to 15 business days after the application collection period; 7. Remove real estate brokerage fees from the list of eligible closing costs; 8. Direct administration to outsource the eligibility review process; and 9. Direct staff to edit the draft policy documents to reflect these amendments. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Mortgage help: city loans up to $25,000
motions.summary: The city created a mortgage assistance program offering homebuyers loans of up to $25,000, prioritized by job type and then by lower household income.
motions.impact: If you're buying a home in Eagle Mountain, you can apply for up to $25,000 toward the purchase. Households of six or more earning up to $151,800 may qualify, and an outside reviewer will check eligibility.

motions.impact: If it moves ahead, you'd see six new directional signs around the city. Nothing else changes.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as the Berry Property from Agriculture to Foothill Residential
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as the Berry Property from Agriculture to Foothill Residential. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Berry property rezoned for foothill homes
motions.summary: The city rezoned the land known as the Berry property from agriculture to foothill residential, opening it to housing.
motions.impact: The land can now be developed as foothill housing instead of staying farmland. Neighbors should expect a housing project to move forward there, though the motion sets no timeline or number of homes.

motions.summary: The council took up a matching change to the general plan land use map for the Berry property.
motions.impact: This is the paperwork that lines the city's long-range map up with the zoning change on the same land. On its own, it changes nothing you would see.

motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 17.10 Definitions, and Sections 16.35.090 Privacy Fencing, 17.60.120 General Fencing Provisions, and 17.60.130 Chain Link Fencing. motions.summary: The council took up changes to the city's fence rules, covering definitions, privacy fencing, general fencing standards, and chain link fencing.
motions.impact: Fence rules govern what you can put up around your own yard. The motion does not spell out what changed, so check the current code with the city before building a fence.

motions.summary: The council delayed a decision on a new rule that would require a mixture of lot sizes in developments.
motions.impact: Nothing changes for now. The rule would apply to developers laying out new subdivisions, not to existing homeowners, and it comes back to the council later.

Equestrian Center be changed from Permitted to Special; b. The Windmills line be amended to include language stating “Windmills, if exclusively secondary/accessory to an AG use”; c. motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code, Repealing and Replacing Chapter 17.40 Industrial Zone, and Amending Chapters 17.20 Agriculture Zone and 17.38 Commercial Storage Zone with the following changes: 1. 17.20.020 Land Use Table: a. Equestrian Center be changed from Permitted to Special; b. The Windmills line be amended to include language stating “Windmills, if exclusively secondary/accessory to an AG use”; c. Utility, Public or Private be changed from Permitted to blank; 2. 17.37.020 Land Use Table Utility, Public or Private be changed from Permitted to blank; and 3. 17.38.060(E) retain the maximum of six allowed number of moving vehicles, and include “(e.g., vans, box trucks, trailers, etc.). Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Industrial zone rules replaced; farm zone tweaked
motions.summary: The city replaced its industrial zone rules and adjusted the agriculture and commercial storage zones, requiring special approval for equestrian centers and capping moving vehicles at six.
motions.impact: If you run or plan an equestrian center, a storage yard, or an industrial business, the rules for what you can build and how many trucks you can keep on site have changed. Most residents will notice nothing.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as the Enyo Battery Property from the Airpark Zone to the Agriculture Zone
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Rezoning Certain Lands Known as the Enyo Battery Property from the Airpark Zone to the Agriculture Zone. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Enyo battery site rezoned back to agriculture
motions.summary: The city rezoned the land known as the Enyo battery property from the airpark zone to the agriculture zone.
motions.impact: The site is now farm-zoned rather than airpark-zoned, which narrows what can be built there. Nothing changes for residents day to day.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapters 17.25 Residential Zones, 17.35 Commercial Zones, and 17.37 Business Park Zones with the following change: 1. The amendment in 17.25.050(G), 17.35.050(G), and 17.37.050(G) be amended to read, “No permanent structures near natural washes shall be built in the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side, as measured out from the top of the wash, whichever is greater, to be determined by the City Engineer or designee. Additionally, no earthwork, excavation, or earth removal shall occur within the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side of the top-of-bank as determined by determined by the City Engineer or designee.” Councilmember Clark seconded the motion
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapters 17.25 Residential Zones, 17.35 Commercial Zones, and 17.37 Business Park Zones with the following change: 1. The amendment in 17.25.050(G), 17.35.050(G), and 17.37.050(G) be amended to read, “No permanent structures near natural washes shall be built in the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side, as measured out from the top of the wash, whichever is greater, to be determined by the City Engineer or designee. Additionally, no earthwork, excavation, or earth removal shall occur within the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side of the top-of-bank as determined by determined by the City Engineer or designee.” Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Bigger no-build buffer around natural washes
motions.summary: The council took up a rule barring permanent buildings and earthwork within 75 feet of a wash's center flowline, or 50 feet from its bank, whichever is greater.
motions.impact: If your lot backs onto a dry wash, this limits how close you can build or dig. It applies to homes, shops, and business parks alike, with the city engineer measuring the buffer.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving an Agreement for Consulting Services for the Downtown Master Plan. The proposed resolution approves an agreement for consulting services for the Downtown Master Plan. The City Council received presentations from three firms in the earlier work session and selected their preferred firm during this scheduled item.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving an Agreement for Consulting Services with MHTN Architects for the Downtown Master Plan. Councilmember Clark seconded the motion.
motions.headline: MHTN Architects hired to plan a downtown
motions.summary: The city hired MHTN Architects to create the Downtown Master Plan, choosing the firm after hearing pitches from three competing firms.
motions.impact: Nothing changes on the ground yet. This hires the firm that will draft the city's vision for a downtown, work that would shape what eventually gets built there.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, as Approved by the Redevelopment Agency of Eagle Mountain City, as the Official Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan for the Project Area and Directing that Notice of the Adoption be Given as Required by Statute. Economic Development Director Evan Berrett presented the item. The proposed ordinance will allow for the creation of the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area. This Plan is the end result of a comprehensive evaluation of the types of appropriate land uses and economic development for the land, which lies within twenty-four parcels in the City. The north parcels are south of 4000 North, north of Pole Canyon Blvd, and east of Tyson Pkwy. The south parcel is south of 1000 North and east of Pony Express Pkwy. The Plan is intended to define the method and means of the Project Area from its current state to a higher and better use.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, as Approved by the Redevelopment Agency of Eagle Mountain City, as the Official Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan for the Project Area and Directing that Notice of the Adoption be Given as Required by Statute. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion.
motions.headline: Triple Tail redevelopment plan adopted
motions.summary: The city adopted the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, covering 24 parcels, to steer that land toward new development and economic uses.
motions.impact: If you live near 4000 North and Pole Canyon Boulevard east of Tyson Parkway, or south of 1000 North east of Pony Express Parkway, expect the city to actively pursue development on the land around you.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Tract Development Agreement. City Attorney Marcus Draper presented the item. The proposed ordinance approves the Tract Development Agreement, which covers approximately 672 acres of land distributed among 2 different parcels. One of the parcels is located near the Meta, Google, and QTS sites. The other parcel abuts Industrial Planning Area 2 of the Firefly development in the southwestern portion of the City. Applicant representative Keely Ambrose addressed the Council regarding concerns around buffering, the addition of property, benchmarks, and length of the agreement.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Tract Development Agreement with the following change: 1. The last three sentences in Section 4.12 are removed and replaced with, “If Additional Property is annexed into this Agreement pursuant to this Section 4.12, then such future property shall be buffered as required by the Applicable Rules. This paragraph does not apply to any property located outside the City limits unless it is annexed into the City.” Councilmember Gray seconded the motion.
motions.headline: 672-acre development deal near the data centers
motions.summary: The council took up a development agreement covering about 672 acres on two parcels, one near the Meta, Google, and QTS sites and one beside the Firefly area.
motions.impact: This touches landowners and neighbors near the data center campuses and in the southwest near Firefly. The council rewrote the buffering language so it only binds land once that land is annexed into the city.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving a Professional Services Agreement with REDKOR Brand Campaigns to Create a Marketing Plan. This item was discussed after item 14.A. Communications Manager Tyler Maffitt presented the item. Communications Manager Tyler Maffitt presented the item. Eagle Mountain City is pursuing this contract to develop a more comprehensive and cohesive messaging strategy. The goal is to ensure that all communications, whether related to tourism, economic development, or other City initiatives, are consistent, agreed upon, and effective in reaching their intended audiences. This strategic approach is intended to achieve outcomes and fully unify the City's voice while enhancing its overall communication efforts now and into the future.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving an Agreement with Identity Signs for Six Wayfinding Signs. Finance Management Analyst Terrence Dela Pena presented the item. Wayfinding signs currently exist throughout the City; these are deteriorating due to exposure to weather conditions and the usual wear and tear for their allowable functionality and appearance. Some signs have become problematic for visibility issues, while others are needed to direct the public to new parks such as Smith Ranch Park and other existing city parks. The new wayfinding signs will adopt the new branding logo and colors, which will support the overall look and feel the City Council, residents, and Staff want for the community. The panels are adjustable and can be changed depending on which city facilities or amenities need to be highlighted. The timeline will depend primarily on the availability of the wood post, and staff hopes the signs can be installed before the end of fall this year.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wood moved to deny the approval of a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, for an Agreement with Identity Signs for Six Wayfinding Signs with instructions to staff to find a more durable material for the signs and a lower installation cost option. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion.
motions.headline: New park and city signs sent back to staff
motions.summary: The council rejected a contract with Identity Signs for six new wayfinding signs and told staff to find sturdier materials and cheaper installation.
motions.impact: The aging signs directing you to parks like Smith Ranch Park stay as they are for now, and new ones will not go up this fall as staff had hoped.

motions.headline: New fence and buffer rules, and a way to force repairs
motions.summary: The council approved fencing and buffer standards, barring berms or hedges as substitutes for required fences, defining split-rail fencing, and letting the city treat unsafe fences as nuisances.
motions.impact: If your fence is falling apart, built from broken or flammable scrap, or put up to spite a neighbor, the city can now declare it a nuisance and make you fix it. Most homeowners are unaffected.

Legislative Priorities List Director of Legislative Affairs Clifford Strachan updated the Council on the status of items on the legislative priorities list. He has completed research on second class city requirements and asked the Council their preferred method to identiff and address completed items. The City Council considered the process for ongoing and completed items and approved marking the second class city requirements as complete. Councilmember Curtis recommended adding specific criteria to Municipal Code standards to clarifu requirements and circumstances under which exceptions would be considered. Mr. Mumford explained that the Planning Department is working on small corrections to Municipal Code that they have identified but also desire to prioritize changes requested by the Council. Councilmember Curtis and Mayor Pro Tempore Wright requested that discussion items be added to this section of the agenda regarding potential sections of Municipal Code being placed under review prior to Planning staff drafting the changes, in order to provide direction. Mr. Mumford expressed concem about bypassing the Plar¡ring Commission in the process but said staff can reach out to the Council in instances where the standards are vague or unclear. Staff intends to seek feedback on complex items such as multifamily and commercial design standards for direction before Commission review" Potential code amendments are approved to be placed on the agenda by the Mayor. Mr. Strachan noted that there are varying preferences regarding desired amendments and stated the importance of recognizing the particular roles assigned to each parfy. He advised the Council to staff to bring forth their best ideas, information, and practices, and make adjustments as the Council directs, but to not cut off the ideas before they come. Mayor Pro Tempore Wright stated that in light of the directives from the State, he has concerns with the nuances and flexibilities in Municipal Code, particularly with Title 16. As much as he respects the Planning Commission, they are not professional planners and it is at the purview of the Council to determine the review authority. He is nervous to grant broad discretion in some cases and advocated reviewing applicable instances in Titles 16 and 17. Councilmember Curtis concurred and said he desires to give feedback on areas where the Council has discretion. Mr. Jerome explained that staff can misunderstand when Councilmembers are stating an opinion veÍsus when they are providing direction. Administrator Items are intended to allow the Council to provide direction to staff as a body in a public setting. Staff will make changes as directed by the Council during their review, regardless of the staff recommendation. He beseeched staff and the Council to trust in the process and to respect each other's roles. Residents are encouraged to dispose of items in the dumpsters. Residents with items that cannot be dumped will be provided with a pass to the Intermountain Regional Landfill in Fairfield. • Sandbag resources are being provided through Eagle Mountain City until flooding risks subside in the community. Interested residents can retrieve as many as 30 sandbags per household at City Hall or the Community Development building. Sand is available at White Hills Park, the Rodeo Grounds, North Ranch Park and Silverlake Park. • Homeowners are encouraged to wait before watering their lawns for the year. Help the City achieve its water conservation goals while better managing our water utility systems. Wait to water until temperatures are consistently warmer. • Residents who don’t use social media to stay in touch with the City are encouraged to sign up for the City’s text notification system. motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Eagle Mountain City Transportation Master Plan. City Engineer Chris Trusty presented the changes as discussed during the work session. Councilmember Wright recommended tabling the item to resolve concerns and finalize details. Councilmember Love said she sees no need for Old Airport Road to follow the proposed trajectory if the future freeway is being relocated. She would like to review and better understand the impacts of the proposed changes in alignment before approving the plan and agrees that it would be beneficial to have Old Airport Road and the future freeway lined with commercial uses, open space, or decorative features to provide buffering for residential areas. Discussion ensued regarding uncertainty with land acquisition, the potential need to abandon certain areas of the road once the freeway is completed, and possible solutions. Mr. Trusty stated that he is unable to move forward with the impact fees facility plan until the Transportation Master Plan is approved and a landowner has been waiting on the finalization of the plan to be able to sell property. He recognized the Council’s desire to get the details of the plan correct but noted master plans generally exclude the finer details of the projects. He confirmed that the Council will be reviewing and voting upon the expansion of Old Airport Road independent of this approval. It might prove beneficial to contact the property owners to evaluate the likelihood of the City being able to purchase the land necessary to change the alignment. Mayor Westmoreland explained the challenges the City faces with future transportation in this area for Old Airport Road and the future freeway. Discussion determined to table the item and to assign two Councilmembers to work with staff and the consultants on amending the plan.
motions.motion: Councilmember Burnham moved to table an ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Eagle Mountain City Transportation Master Plan to the next meeting. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion. motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Eagle Mountain City Vision Statement, Mission Statement, and Strategic Goals. Economic Development Director Evan Berrett presented the item and reviewed the elements of strategic planning. Staff and the City Council determined to review the mission statement at a future meeting and discussed and amended the draft vision and strategic goals as follows: Vision: Eagle Mountain is a safe, growing city with a small town feel that serves families and individuals by creating reliable services and infrastructure, cultivating economic and recreational opportunities, and harmonizing protected space with the flourishing of all life. Strategic Goals: 1. Diverse Economic Growth. Eagle Mountain is home to businesses of all sizes spanning several industries resulting in an expanded tax base, convenient access for all residents to essential goods and services, and growth of employment opportunities for workers at any stage of their careers. 2. Robust Infrastructure Networks. Eagle Mountain has expanded its infrastructure capacities to comfortably accommodate the demands of a larger population by improving transportation connections and infrastructure standards alongside state and regional partners, augmenting network capabilities, and implementing maintenance and replacement programs for all infrastructure. 3. Unique Reputational Evolution. Eagle Mountain is known and respected for its commitments toward, and achievements in, meeting the expectations of residents through efforts to embrace its family-centric and rural heritage, engaging in creative solutions to address resident needs, and its contributions to the prosperity of the state. 4. Proactive Generational Planning. Eagle Mountain is a balanced, intergenerational city that has proactively managed its growth, resulting in quality home-ownership opportunities for residents; a redundant and reliable water supply; and gathering places and amenities that provide for the social, educational, recreational, and health care needs of its residents. 5. Interactive Environmental Stewardship. Eagle Mountain has interlaced the preservation of the natural environment; the protection of native wildlife; and the promotion of outdoor recreation through the expansion of permanent, convenient, and interconnected trail networks; conservation of open spaces and natural features; and protection of historic sites significant to our heritage 6. Dynamic Service Enhancement. Eagle Mountain is a full-service community that delivers extraordinary services and amenities to residents by attracting and retaining passionate employees, innovating throughout the organization to increase efficiency and remain fiscally conservative, and developing highly responsive communication channels to improve resident experiences.
motions.motion: Councilmember Gray moved to approve a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Eagle Mountain City Vision Statement, Mission Statement, and Strategic Goals as discussed. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion. He is uncomfortable making a goodwill gesture with tax money paid by the residents. Councilmember Gray acknowledged that although he does not feel the City is to blame, neither does he think the applicant is completely at fault, as they were required to clean up debris left by other people. Councilmember Burnham conceded Councilmember Gray’s point but agreed with concerns about passing the expense of the developer’s taxes to residents. Councilmember Wright said while he appreciates the applicant resolving the issue, the agreement with the City required the dedication of the land. Nevertheless, the applicant had the ability to monitor and mitigate the taxes compared to the residents that had no ability to weigh in on the issue. Councilmember Love said she understands the desire to offer a gesture of goodwill to the developer; however, it would set a precedence that could become problematic. Councilmember Gray clarified that his intention is not to pay the taxes but to show courtesy and properly credit the developer for their positive contributions to the City during interactions on future projects.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Enacting Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 2.17 Appointed Officers, and Amending Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 2.27 Board Appointment Process. Ms. Kofoed reviewed the item as presented during work session. She read the email Councilmember Curtis sent to the Council that was mentioned during work session with his suggested changes to the amendment. The Council discussed the proposed amendment and determined to approve the following changes: • EMMC 2.17.010 Process for Appointing Officers – In accordance with Utah Code Ann. § 10-3-9, the mayor, with the advice and consent of the city council, shall appoint a qualified person to the office of city recorder, city treasurer, city attorney and city engineer. If Eagle Mountain City creates a municipal fire or police department, the police chief and fire chief shall also be appointed officers. All appointed officers shall continue in office until their successors are appointed and qualified. All appointments of officers designated herein shall follow the process as outlined in EMMC 2.27 Appointment Process. • EMMC Chapter 2.27 Appointment Process: o 2.27.010 Definitions - “Statutorily appointed” shall mean any position designated in EMMC 2.17.010 Appointed Officers. o 2.27.020 Appointment – Unless otherwise designated, the mayor shall appoint all advisory board members, statutorily appointed officers, and planning commission members with the advice and consent of the city council. o 2.27.030 Posting of Positions – Notice of all empty or expiring advisory board, statutorily appointed positions, or planning commission members shall be posted on the city webpage, or other method suitable to provide notice to the public, for a minimum of ten days. The notice shall include a description of the position and provide details for the submission of an application or resume for the position. The mayor shall compile and evaluate all applications or resumes for the position. o 2.27.040 Notice to Council – Not less than three (3) days prior to publicly noticing the possible appointment or reappointment of any person to an advisory board, planning commission, or statutorily appointed position, the mayor shall provide to each member of the city council the name, and application or resume if available, of each person the mayor is considering appointing to an advisory board, planning commission, or statutorily appointed position. Members of the city council may individually provide the mayor with feedback or recommendations regarding each potential appointment. o 2.27.050 Removal – An advisory board or planning commission member may be removed with or without cause by the mayor with the advice and consent of the city council.

motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Public Infrastructure District Policy. Councilmember Curtis expressed concern with the risks associated with Public Infrastructure Districts (PIDs), allowing developers to oversee resident taxes, and the potential abuse of inflated reimbursement rates. As he has no intention of applying a PID to a residential development, he would prefer not to have associated standards in Municipal Code. Councilmembers Wright and Love concurred with not approving PIDs for residential developments. Mayor Westmoreland noted the benefit of the additional oversight and risk reduction measures of invested parties. City Attorney Jeremy Cook clarified the reason for placing the item on the agenda was to identify Council concerns to be able to address the issues and establish approval criteria in the governing document. Section 4 provides for the Council to deny a PID for any reason. PIDs could allow for improvements desired in the City that would otherwise be not viable financially. Discussion ensued regarding concerns regarding: • The impact of the cost of the PID on house affordability; • The potential for homebuyers to not understand the higher tax rate when purchasing their home; • The impact on the ability of residents to sell their homes; • The PID cost increasing as the value of the home increases; • Development funding mechanisms; • Placing the burden of improvements and benefits to the overall City on a specific group of residents; and • Details of the bond payments. Councilmember Love requested additional information regarding commercial PIDs. City Administrator Paul Jerome recommended any PIDs approved in the City have an economic development component. He does not foresee a circumstance in which the City would find a residential PID to be beneficial.
motions.motion: Councilmember Love moved to table a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Public Infrastructure Policy inviting staff, if desired, to bring back the item as a commercial economic development policy and tool that excludes residential development. AMENDED MOTION: Councilmember Love moved to table a resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Public Infrastructure Policy. Councilmember Curtis seconded the motion. MOTION – Amended Preliminary Plat Items 14.A., 14.B., and 14.C. were presented and discussed concurrently. Planning Manager Robert Hobbs presented the items. The applicant wishes to develop 98 single- family detached units and 40 twin-home units in lieu of the approved 148 duplex units. He explained that the new plan will: • Reduce the number of housing units by ten. • Add lot lines to twin home lots to allow the units to be sold individually. • Add single-family lots to create a better transition to the east, south, and west. • Add open space to the backyards of single-family lots. • Add a half basketball court to increase overall amenities. • Upgrade architecture on the clubhouse. • Allow the homebuyer the option to add accessory dwelling units (ADUs) or to remove the basement from the single-family home design plan. The amenities plan exceeds the requisite amenity points; however, it provides a lower open space acreage than required. On August 16, 2022, the trail was intentionally omitted from the plan. On July 26th, the Planning Commission unanimously voted to recommend that Council approve the Eagle Height Village project modification(s), contingent upon development/developer compliance with the following conditions/changes: 1. In the MDA page 6, section 2.2, change the final sentence to “The elevation and design of buildings must be consistent with the previously approved building elevations and newly proposed building elevations as illustrated in Exhibit E;” and 2. On page 7, change Section 2.5 to “ADUs are allowed in the project as a way to encourage additional affordable housing options in the City.” Councilmember Love stated she would like to stipulate in the agreement that the elevations are required to meet Municipal Code standards. Assistant City Administrator/Community Development Director Steve Mumford explained that recent State Legislative changes severely limit the abilities of cities to regulate the architecture standards for single-family homes outside of a development agreement. The City Attorney and he discussed Section 14.3.1 and they recommend the addition of verbiage to clearly indicate that with the transference of the remainder of the project Fieldstone Homes assumes the responsibility for the development of the amenities and parks and open space. He recommended adding parks 4, 5, and 6 to the assignability clause and specifying pool accessibility in the agreement. Applicant representative Jason Harris with Fieldstone Homes said the elevations are from their Brylee Farms project which underwent review prior to the legislative changes limiting architectural standard requirements for single-family homes. He explained the parks were excluded from the agreement because the original developer is developing the parks and the lots. They will be responsible for pool and clubhouse installation and construction. He confirmed that they understand that building permits for the homes will not be issued until the park improvements are completed. They have agreed to purchase the lots after the initial developer has completed their portion of the development including the parks. A basketball halfcourt has been installed that was not included as a requirement in the previous agreement. The single-family homes will have an optional basement that can be excluded to reduce the cost of the units. Basement accessory dwelling units (ADUs) will be an option with the twin home design. They intend to follow the setback requirements for the RC Zone and he is amenable to the motion to amend the rear setback for the single-family homes from 15 feet to 20 feet. Mr. Mumford explained the project has a trail in the center of the project to connect to the park. The language in the agreement allows the developer to work with neighboring properties to provide a safe route to schools. Even though the City was unable reach an agreement with the adjacent property owner, an additional trail providing pedestrian access to schools or fee-in-lieu is still required. Councilmember Love suggested retaining Section 2.4 from the original agreement until it can be verified that a safe school route has been provided. Discussion ensued regarding whether to retain the verbiage requiring the trail, the portion and location of trail to require until the installation of Old Airport Road in that area, and trail requirements and agreement reimbursement options for the trial on the adjacent properties. Mayor Westmoreland opened the public hearing at 8:44 p.m. As there were no comments, he closed the hearing. Discussion clarified the purpose and intent of the Planning Commission's recommended conditions of approval. Councilmember Gray noted that the desire of the Council is for the amenities and the pool and clubhouse to be open to all residents in the old and new portions of the development.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to approve an ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, approving the first amendment to the Eagle Heights Village Master Development Plan with the following conditions: 1. Leave 2.4 Trail as written and clarify it pertains to the trail connection on the north end of the development on the south side of Eagle Mountain Boulevard; 2. In the MDA page 6, section 2.2, change the final sentence to “The elevation and design of buildings must be consistent with the previously approved building elevations and newly proposed building elevations as illustrated in Exhibit E;” 3. On page 7, change Section 2.5 to “ADUs are allowed in the project as a way to encourage additional affordable housing options in the City.” 4. Change the rear setback from 15 feet to 20 feet; and 5. Clarifying that all amenities, parks, and open spaces are available to each of the residents in the entire development. Councilmember Burnham seconded the motion. motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain City Municipal Code Section 17.15.030 Planning Commission Organization. Mr. Cook presented the item. He reviewed the proposed amendment to add an alternate Planning Commission member and the appointment process. The Planning Commission reviewed the amendment on June 14 and voted to recommend approval with changes to allow the alternate member to vote if a regular member is absent or if a regular member recuses themselves from an item, and a change to set a term of three years, or until appointed as a regular member of the Commission. The proposed amendment includes these recommended changes. Mr. Cook explained he had drafted the standards to allow the alternate member to function in a training role until appointed. However, he supports the Planning Commission's suggestions as they better understand the needs and function of the Commission. Mayor Pro Tempore Love concurred with the Planning Commission's recommendation for a set term for alternates with the option to reappoint individuals as alternate members. Mr. Cook suggested changing “the alternate member shall serve a term of three years or until appointed as a regular member of the planning commission or removed in accordance with subsection G” to “the alternate member shall serve a term of three years unless appointed as a regular member of the planning commission or removed in accordance with subsection G” to clarify the intent is for the alternate to be appointed to the Commission during rather than after a three-year term. Councilmember Gray suggested adjusting the Planning Commission appointment schedule to allow for two appointments each year. Discussion ensued regarding the current terms of Planning Commissioners. Councilmember Curtis said regarding the requirement to notify the Council of board appointees prior to public notification is most important for the Planning Commission. He suggested adding verbiage that Planning Commission appointments are considered board appointments for the purpose of posting and noticing and shall comply with all posting and noticing requirements in EMMC 2.27. He believes it is within the purview of the Council to legislate the appointment process. Councilmember Burnham stated she has struggled with the requested amendments as she thinks it is prescribing to the Mayor how to make appointments, which is a role that statute delegates to the Mayor. The Council makes laws that would better function as processes due to difficulties created in codifying the requirements. She noted that 2.27 needs further clarification as to which City groups are included or excluded from the requirements. Discussion ensued regarding whether Planning Commissioners can or should be considered board appointments as governed by EMMC 2.27. Mayor Pro Tempore Love and Councilmember Wright both advocated for the posting and notification requirements to be codified rather than a process.
motions.motion: Mayor Pro Tempore Love moved to table an ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, amending the Eagle Mountain City Municipal Code Section 17.15.030 Planning Commission Organization with direction to Mr. Cook to bring the item back to the next possible agenda with the following changes: 1. Section C – Allow regular and alternate terms to be shortened or lengthened at the purview of the Council to stagger the appointments to fill two positions each year; 2. Section C – The alternate member shall serve a term of three years unless appointed as a regular member of the Planning Commission or removed in accordance with subsection G; and 3. Replace Section E with, “The Planning Commission appointments are considered board appointments for purposes of posting and noticing and shall comply with all posting and noticing requirements in EMMC 2.27 Board Appointment Process.” Councilmember Curtis seconded the motion. Councilmember Burnham noted that the Council will provide feedback and direction to staff regarding tabled items, but a motion to table an item typically does not have specific directions to staff within the motion. Mayor Pro Tempore Love withdrew her motion.

motions.item_title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain City Municipal Code Chapter 13.75 Eagle Mountain City Storm Water Ordinance. This item was discussed after item 20.A. Mr. Cook presented the item. The proposed ordinance updates the City's stormwater ordinance to clarify procedures and requirements for stormwater management plans and long-term stormwater management agreements related to properties with personal stormwater facilities. The main change requires stormwater management plans be submitted with business license applications to ensure State compliance. Councilmember Curtis recommended adding exemption criteria to the standards. Councilmember Wright concurred. Mr. Cook explained that it is difficult to anticipate individual circumstances. The intent is to allow flexibility and evaluation of individual situations. Exemption criteria could be added to the chapter when the standards return to approve the consolidated fee schedule.

ORDINANCE/PUBLIC HEARING – An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Final Budget Amendments for Fiscal Year 2021- 2022. Finance Director Kimberly Ruesch presented the item. She reviewed the impact fee payments and transfers and explained that $600,000 is included as a placeholder to reimburse developer overpayment for streetlight installation. She requested an additional $146,500 be added to the budget to cover the cost of issuing the 2022 series sales tax bond, which will be covered by the proceeds of the bond. 16.B. ORDINANCE/PUBLIC HEARING – An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Budget totaling $121,380,554 and the Certified Tax Rate. Ms. Ruesch presented the final budget and certified tax rate. An additional $7,500 is requested for information services to automate data entry processes to reduce labor costs. The City’s total taxable value increased by almost two billion dollars over the past year, mostly due to the Meta development. As a result, the certified tax rate has been reduced. The new property tax is approximately $29 per year per $100,000 of value for a primary residence. Approximately ten years ago, rates generated around $98 in property tax per $100,000 of value. Ms. Ruesch explained the $1,000 increase for Information Services reflects an increase in the cost of social media archival services. The increase of $3,000 for text messaging service will allow the City to send shut-off notifications via text messages rather than door tags, as well as individualized messaging to specified groups of residents. Discussion clarified the fleet size, usage, expenditures, transfers, and purchasing. Mayor Pro Tempore Love recommended changes to clarify that the days and hours of the day restrictions are required in State code, to determine financial liability, and to prohibit fireworks within 75 feet of undeveloped land or buildings under construction. Councilmember Gray suggested requiring a distance greater than 75-feet. Mr. Cook suggested including that adult residents are liable for fires caused by the actions of minor dependents. The State requires the City to have a map of restricted areas which could include the prohibited distances from certain areas. United Fire Authority Battalion Chief Embret Fossum stated that a distance requirement from undeveloped properties would create an enforcement burden; removing neighborhoods from restricted areas once they are fully built out is preferable. He is concerned that codifying restrictions not indicated on the map could cause confusion. motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Establishing Fireworks Restrictions for 2022. Mayor Westmoreland noted the difficulty in defining firework restrictions to protect residents and the City due to the unique characteristics and abundance of natural open spaces areas. Unified Fire Authority (UFA) representatives have provided input in determining firework restrictions. High wind and weather also impact fire safety. Mr. Cook verified the City can only prohibit geographical boundaries and may not include weather restrictions in the prohibitions. Councilmember Curtis recommended employing an informational campaign to educate residents concerning aerial firework dangers and weather impacts. Councilmember Love requested to review the prohibited locations to verify the reasonability of the restriction to ensure identical standards were applied to all areas. Councilmember Wright suggested approving the item with direction to staff to further evaluate Brandon Park, Sage Park, and Evans Ranch to determine if the subdivisions have a central area deemed safe for fireworks. Director of Administrative Services/City Recorder Fionnuala Kofoed explained firework restrictions are required to be provided to the County by May 1st. UFA Battalion Chief Embret Fossum stated that his understanding is that the restrictions must be set prior to May 1st, and cannot be amended afterward other than circumstances qualifying for the emergency clause. Mr. Cook explained Utah Code 15A-5-202 is an amendment to International Fire Code and cities must be in compliance with both documents when setting fire restrictions. Discussion ensued regarding the following: • The clarification that the proposed map is based upon staff and UFA recommendations and it is the purview of the Council to remove or add restricted areas; • Natural landscape and framed houses in neighborhoods undergoing construction increase fire hazards; • Enforcement and confusion with approved location considerations; • Restrictions assisting with establishing resident liability; • Historical data used as consideration for the restriction map may no longer be relevant if the characteristics of the region have changed; • Salt Lake City restricts fireworks in all areas east of 1300 East; • Scheduling to evaluate the map in-depth prior to the approval of restrictions for 2023; • Pursuing the City offering alternative forms of celebration; • The desire to establish uniform standards; • Law Enforcement discretion when issuing citations and liability restitution; and • Codifying permanently allowed and restricted areas and perimeter standards. Councilmember Love recommended including clarification that residents are liable for fire damage regardless of igniting fireworks in an allowed or prohibited area. Councilmember Wright believes the 2019 map has negative impacts on some residents. Nevertheless, the recommended restrictions represent a plan with previously vetted developments that has been implemented in the past and would allow the item to move forward within the requisite timeframe. He feels passionately that the proposed map should be reviewed in-depth and updated prior to approving firework restriction areas for 2023. He encouraged residents to be responsible and not ignite fireworks in restricted areas due to the high fire dangers. Ms. Kofoed suggested permitting fireworks at completed park parking lots within the restricted developments if deemed appropriate by staff. She explained that staff had been operating under the assumption that fireworks would be restricted City-wide this year until they received notification from UFA desiring an updated map. Councilmember Curtis stated he had made potential amendments to the firework restrictions map to allow fireworks in some subdivisions. Discussion ensued regarding opening City park parking lots to residents for fireworks uses, clarifying that church parking lots are private property and should not be used for fireworks, and providing information to the public to promote safety.
